steps.body: Conics run the solar system. **Kepler's first law**: every planet orbits the Sun on an **ellipse** with the Sun at ONE focus (not the center). The orbit's eccentricity says how oval it is — and the same e-scale from this course classifies every path through space.

widget.prompt: Earth's orbit is nearly circular. Slide the eccentricity down to 0.2 and watch where the focus sits.
widget.successFeedback: At low eccentricity the ellipse is almost a circle, but the focus is still NOT the centre — and that is Kepler's first law: the Sun sits at a focus, not the middle. Earth's real eccentricity is 0.017, which is why the orbit looks circular while the seasons still differ in length.
widget.explorationFeedback: Slide across a range first; the focus-versus-centre distinction is easiest to see while the shape is changing.
widget.lowFeedback: Below 0.2 — even rounder than the target.

explanationVariants: Earth's orbital eccentricity is about 0.017 — very close to 0, so Earth's orbit is nearly a circle.
e ≈ 0.017 places Earth at the almost-circular end of the ellipse scale.

widget.prompt: Earth's orbit has eccentricity e ≈ 0.017. This means its orbit is:

options.label: nearly a perfect circle
options.feedback: Right — e near 0 means barely oval; Earth's orbit is almost circular.

options.label: a long, thin ellipse
options.feedback: That would be e near 1. e ≈ 0.017 is nearly circular.

options.label: a hyperbola
options.feedback: Hyperbolas need e > 1. e ≈ 0.017 is a nearly circular ellipse.

steps.body: Comets show the other extreme. Halley's Comet has e ≈ 0.97 — a long, cigar-shaped ellipse swinging far out and back. Objects with **e ≥ 1** (parabolic or hyperbolic paths) visit ONCE and never return: they aren't bound to the Sun.

explanationVariants: An object on a hyperbolic path (e > 1) is unbound — it passes the Sun once and leaves forever.
e > 1 means an open orbit: a single flyby, no return.

widget.prompt: An interstellar object passes the Sun on a path with e = 1.2. It will:

options.label: pass once and never return (unbound)
options.feedback: Right — e > 1 is a hyperbola, an open, one-time path.

options.label: orbit forever like a planet
options.feedback: Only e < 1 (ellipse) gives a closed, repeating orbit. e = 1.2 is unbound.

options.label: crash into the Sun
options.feedback: e = 1.2 is a hyperbolic flyby — it swings past once and leaves.

explanationVariants: A satellite dish is a parabola (e = 1): its reflective property (Ch1) sends every parallel incoming ray to the single focus, where the receiver sits.
The parabola's reflective property concentrates parallel rays at the focus.

widget.prompt: A satellite dish concentrates parallel incoming signals at one point. Its cross-section is a:

options.label: parabola
options.feedback: Right — the parabola reflects parallel rays to its focus (the receiver).

options.label: circle
options.feedback: Circles don't focus parallel rays to a point. The dish is a parabola.

options.label: hyperbola
options.feedback: The parallel-to-focus property belongs to the parabola (e = 1).

explanationVariants: A comet with e = 0.97 is a highly elongated ELLIPSE (still < 1), so it's bound and returns — just on a very long, stretched loop.
e = 0.97 < 1 keeps it a (very stretched) ellipse: bound, periodic, returning.
hints: Below 1 means which conic — bound or unbound?

widget.prompt: A comet has orbital eccentricity e = 0.97. Its orbit is:

options.label: a very elongated ellipse (bound, it returns)
options.feedback: Right — e < 1 stays an ellipse; highly stretched, but bound and periodic.

options.label: a hyperbola (it never returns)
options.feedback: Hyperbolas need e > 1. e = 0.97 < 1 is still a (stretched) ellipse.

options.label: a perfect circle
options.feedback: A circle is e = 0. e = 0.97 is a very elongated ellipse.

takeaways: Kepler: planets ride ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
e < 1 orbits are bound and repeat; e ≥ 1 paths escape forever.
Parabolic reflectors focus parallel rays — conic geometry, applied.
steps.teaser: Course complete — the conic sections, from locus to orbit.

concept.body: Orbits are conics with the Sun at a focus (Kepler). e < 1 → bound ellipse (returns); e ≥ 1 → open path (escapes). Parabolic reflectors focus parallel rays.

explanationVariants: e = 0.5 < 1 is a bound ellipse — it returns.
Below 1 means a closed, repeating orbit.

options.label: a bound ellipse that returns
options.feedback: Right — e < 1 is a closed, repeating elliptical orbit.

options.label: an unbound path that escapes
options.feedback: Escape needs e ≥ 1. e = 0.5 is a bound ellipse.

options.label: a straight line
options.feedback: e = 0.5 is an ellipse — bound and returning.
